title: The shroud
hook: plain white cloth, the same for the rich and the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, washing the body, and your line: washed with care. What did you do for someone who couldn't repay you? Today, after the washing, the wrapping. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

How was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, dressed for his burial? 'A'ishah answers in Sahih al-Bukhari, and the answer is almost nothing. Three white sheets of Yemeni cotton. No shirt among them. No turban. The man his followers called the Messenger of Allah, wrapped in plain cloth, the way anyone could be. No embroidery, no rank, no sign of who he'd been. Just cloth, and the body inside it. Today's word is that cloth.
screen: `HOW WAS HE DRESSED FOR BURIAL?` → `THREE WHITE SHEETS.` → `NO SHIRT, NO TURBAN.`

segments.voice: The word is kafan, the shroud. A hadith in Abu Dawud gives the color, in paraphrase: wear white, for it's among the best of your clothes, and shroud your dead in it. So the custom is plain white cloth, wrapped around the washed body, the same whether the person owned a palace or a single room. Whatever they wore in life, they leave in the same white. Two more reports show what that can mean. In al-Bukhari, a man on pilgrimage was thrown from his camel at 'Arafah and killed, still wearing the two plain cloths of ihram. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: wash him with water and lote leaves, and shroud him in his two garments. Don't perfume him, and don't cover his head, for he will be raised on the Day of Rising saying the pilgrim's call. His pilgrim's clothes became his shroud. And from Khabbab, also in al-Bukhari, the story of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, killed at the battle of Uhud. All he left was one cloak. When they covered his head with it, his feet showed. When they covered his feet, his head showed. The Prophet told them to cover his head, and lay a sweet-smelling grass, idhkhir, over his feet. Not enough cloth, and still enough honor. Put those beside the three white sheets, and some readers hear the shroud saying something: that the things that separated people in life, the clothes, the labels, the bank balance, stay behind. What goes into the earth is wrapped in the same white.
screen: `KAFAN: THE SHROUD.` · `WEAR WHITE, SHROUD YOUR DEAD IN IT.` · `A PILGRIM IN HIS TWO CLOTHS.` · `ONE CLOAK, NOT ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of simplicity. Settle, and breathe. Look down at what you're wearing. Think of the things you own that say something about you: a watch, a brand, a title on a badge, a car. Now let each one fall away in your mind, one by one, until there's only you, wrapped in something plain and white. Notice what's still there when the labels are gone. Stay with that. If you pray, you can rest in that plainness before Allah. The bell holds the time.
Kafan. The shroud: plain white cloth, the same for anyone, rich or poor. Today's word.

Your line: everyone in white. Today, when you notice yourself sizing someone up by what they own or wear, remember the plain cloth, and see the person. Tomorrow, the funeral prayer. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: After the washing, Muslims wrap the body in a kafan of plain white cloth, kept simple whatever the person's wealth; a pilgrim who dies in ihram may be shrouded in the ihram garments.

fork.setup: Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr is killed, and his one cloak can't cover both his head and his feet. what do you do?
options: cover his head, and lay idhkhir grass over his feet.
wait until you find more cloth.
fork.reveal: in Khabbab's report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet told them to cover his head and put idhkhir over his feet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a shroud is a funeral formality.
what it means: plain white cloth for anyone, rich or poor, leaving behind what separated people in life.
what a scholar hears: 'A'ishah's three white sheets with no shirt or turban, the pilgrim shrouded in ihram, and Mus'ab's one cloak in al-Bukhari.
